analysis.one_liner: Expands workplace protections against pregnancy discrimination under the Civil Rights Act.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 so that a pregnant worker can prove discrimination by comparing herself to any other applicant or employee at the same employer in similar work whose ability to work is only temporarily limited — a broader and easier comparison to meet than current law allows. It was introduced by a Republican congressman with 15 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant workers and applicants, who would find it easier to win discrimination cases because the law would compare them to a wider pool of coworkers and applicants rather than to a narrow set of 'similar' employees.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the comparator standard in Section 701(k) of the Civil Rights Act, requiring that pregnant workers be treated like 'any other applicants for employment with, or employees employed by, the same employer, in work that is performed under similar working conditions' whose limits are only temporary — replacing the narrower 'similar in their ability' language courts currently apply.
The bill's stated purpose is to expand protections against pregnancy discrimination in the workplace under the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face broader and easier-to-claim liability for pregnancy discrimination, including additional legal and compliance costs for small businesses.

drawbacks.text: Broadening the pool of comparison workers makes it easier to sue, which would raise litigation and compliance costs for employers — costs that small businesses with thin margins would feel most.

The bill only changes the proof standard in discrimination cases; unlike broader legislation considered in the same period, it does not create a right to workplace accommodations for pregnant workers such as modified duties or extra breaks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to pregnant workers is real but modest: it lowers the bar for proving discrimination without changing any underlying workplace obligation. The cost to employers is added legal exposure, which the bill's sponsors evidently judged proportionate; it drew 15 Republican cosponsors and no recorded opposition, but no committee ever weighed the tradeoff in public.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 18, 2019 by Rep. Tim Walberg of Michigan, joined by Reps. Ann Wagner, Elise Stefanik, and Jackie Walorski as original cosponsors.

It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day, and no further action of any kind appears in its record — no report, no markup, no floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Fifteen House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, who face no new pregnancy-discrimination liability, and the status quo of the existing narrower proof standard, which courts and defendants continue to apply.

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand pregnancy discrimination protections.

for.name: 15 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would make it easier for pregnant workers to prove discrimination, exposing employers of all sizes to more lawsuits and settlement costs. Employers' interest in limiting that liability runs against workers' interest in enforceable protection.
